title: Diagonal matrices and the entrywise solution
subtitle: G2 lecture 063000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded, source-grounded mathematical companion: independent derivations, worked examples, vector MathTex, reusable diagrams. Spoken source unchanged.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 063000 · The problem and its setting
slides.lead: When A and B are diagonal in orthonormal eigenbases, the unknown matrix coefficient between eigenvalues a and b is multiplied by a minus b.
body: For diagonal coefficient matrices, the Sylvester equation can be solved entry by entry. The cross-eigenvalue differences determine uniqueness, the available solutions when spectra overlap, and a sharp Frobenius estimate under positive separation. The entrywise formula also connects directly to resolvents and to coordinate-free spectral projections.
slides.takeaway: Diagonal coefficient matrices reduce Sylvester inversion to independent divisions.

slides.title: Write the matrix equation in coordinates
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 063000 · Write the matrix equation in coordinates
slides.lead: Let A be a diagonal matrix with m diagonal entries, and B a diagonal matrix with n diagonal entries.
body: Let X and C be rectangular matrices with m rows and n columns. We want to solve A X minus X B equals C. What is the entry in row i and column j of A X?

Because A is diagonal, it is the i-th diagonal entry of A multiplied by the corresponding entry of X. What about X B? Because B is diagonal, its entry in that position is the entry of X multiplied by the j-th diagonal entry of B.
slides.takeaway: The row index comes from A; the column index comes from B.

slides.title: A complete two-by-two example
slides.lead: A complete calculation with four distinct denominators.
body: Let A=diag(1,4), B=diag(0,3), and C have rows (2,6) and (8,10). The denominator matrix has rows (1,−2) and (4,1), so entrywise division gives X with rows (2,−3) and (2,10).
Direct verification gives AX with rows (2,−3),(8,40) and XB with rows (0,−9),(0,30). Subtraction recovers the stated C exactly.
slides.takeaway: Multiplying the computed X verifies all four Sylvester coefficients.

slides.title: Why uniqueness follows
slides.lead: Suppose X and Y both solve the same equation.
body: Subtract their equations. The difference Z, defined as X minus Y, satisfies A Z minus Z B equals zero. For every entry, the corresponding spectral difference times the entry of Z is zero. If all differences are nonzero, every entry of Z must vanish.

Therefore X equals Y. This is the entire uniqueness proof in diagonal coordinates. Equivalently, the homogeneous Sylvester operator has trivial kernel. Since it acts on a finite-dimensional space of m times n matrix entries, injectivity implies surjectivity. But the explicit division formula already gives surjectivity constructively.
slides.takeaway: Uniqueness is the absence of a nonzero homogeneous matrix block.

slides.title: What if a denominator vanishes?
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 063000 · What if a denominator vanishes?
slides.lead: A zero denominator gives a compatibility condition rather than a division.
body: If aᵢ=bⱼ, the corresponding equation is 0·Xᵢⱼ=Cᵢⱼ. A nonzero right-hand side makes the whole equation unsolvable. If Cᵢⱼ=0, that entry of X is free.
When the shared eigenvalue has multiplicities r for A and s for B, the homogeneous solutions include an arbitrary r-by-s block, contributing rs free scalar parameters.
slides.takeaway: Coincident eigenvalues create explicit compatibility conditions and free entries.

slides.title: A sharp Frobenius estimate
slides.lead: Assume now that the eigenvalues of A and B are separated by a positive distance delta.
body: That means every absolute spectral difference is at least delta. For each entry, the solution formula gives the magnitude of X's entry at most the magnitude of C's entry divided by delta. Square this inequality for each row and column, and add over all entries.
The sum of squared magnitudes of X is at most one over delta squared times the corresponding sum for C. These sums are the squares of the Frobenius norms.
slides.takeaway: Frobenius orthogonality gives constant one under pairwise separation.

slides.title: Why this does not prove the same operator-norm bound
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 063000 · Why this does not prove the same operator-norm bound
slides.lead: It is tempting to use the same argument for the ordinary operator norm.
body: Every entry of X is bounded in magnitude by the corresponding entry of C divided by delta, so perhaps the operator norm of X is at most the operator norm of C divided by delta. That conclusion does not follow from entrywise inequalities.

The operator norm is not monotone under entrywise absolute-value comparison for arbitrary matrices. Changing signs and arrangements of matrix entries can change how they combine when acting on a vector. Our entrywise proof gives the Frobenius bound immediately.
slides.takeaway: Entrywise division alone does not yield the same operator-norm constant.

slides.title: From diagonal entries to spectral projections
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 063000 · From diagonal entries to spectral projections
slides.lead: The formula is not tied to any particular choice of eigenvectors.
body: Let P for each distinct eigenvalue of A denote its orthogonal spectral projection. Let Q for each distinct eigenvalue of B denote the corresponding projection. Every map C can be decomposed into rectangular spectral blocks by placing a projection P on the left and a projection Q on the right.

Summing all of these pieces recovers C because the spectral projections on each side sum to the identity. On one such block, the Sylvester operator multiplies by the scalar eigenvalue of A minus the scalar eigenvalue of B.
slides.takeaway: Spectral projectors recover the formula without a privileged eigenbasis.

slides.title: A resolvent is a special case
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 063000 · A resolvent is a special case
slides.lead: Suppose B is a scalar multiple of the identity, with scalar b.
body: Then X B equals b times X. The equation becomes A X minus b X equals C, or A minus b identity, followed by X, equals C. If b is not an eigenvalue of A, the operator A minus b identity is invertible.

Therefore X is obtained by applying its inverse to C on the left. That inverse is a resolvent operator, up to the conventional sign used when defining a resolvent. In diagonal coordinates, it divides each spectral component by a minus b.
slides.takeaway: Scalar B reduces the equation to a familiar resolvent inverse.

slides.title: Reassemble the inverse
slides.lead: The diagonal division rule is independent of the basis chosen within each eigenspace.
body: Select a spectral block PᵢCQⱼ, divide by the difference aᵢ−bⱼ, and sum. The orthogonal block decomposition makes the Frobenius estimate immediate and sharp. If a difference vanishes, require the corresponding block of C to be zero and retain that block as a free parameter.
Check the concrete 2×2 matrix by multiplication, then distinguish the Frobenius estimate from operator-norm estimates.
slides.takeaway: Every mathematical claim can be checked one spectral coefficient at a time.
